When the member for Nanaimo speaks on defence estimates, we listen to him with respect. Obviously, he has a great and detailed knowledge of the services. When he tells us that, in his opinion, there are savings which could be made in these estimates, I am inclined to agree with him. I believe, however, it will be rather difficult to ascertain just where those savings could be achieved this year. We are spending in the next twelve months the huge sum of $425 million for defence. None of us dispute the necessity for that defence, but when we realize that this figure is greater than the total ordinary expenditure on the Canadian budget in 1939, we also realize how drastic a change has taken place.
That $425 million is a lot of money. How is it going to be spent? We know that in the year 1948-49, $145 million was spent on construction, equipment, supplies and so on. A total of 65,308 contracts were let out. Obviously, this year there will be many more. Despite the denial, which I accept, made the other day in this house by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce about the now rather celebrated study group, I think there remains an unhappy feeling in the minds of many of us that there are some who would like to get their snouts into the patronage trough. I hope the minister will be firm, and will not permit patronage to be shown in this matter of contracts dealing with the Department of National Defence.
It has been said it is government policy to provide the forces estimated to be necessary to defend Canada. Today the minister qualified that somewhat, of course, because we in Canada cannot provide the forces requisite to defend ourselves. We might be able to do so were we to conscript every man, woman and child in the country, and were we to bankrupt ourselves with military expenditures. When the minister states that the defence of Canada is also the defence of the north Atlantic powers, he is right. Defence must be looked upon from that point of view. Yet, in his remarks, I detected what appeared to me to be an illogicality. He said that the best Canadian strength is the collective strength of the north Atlantic powers. There can be no argument against that; it has been said month after month during the past year. Yet, surely, collective strength implies that commitments have been made collectively to defend ourselves collectively; but earlier the minister stated we had made no specific commitment under the North Atlantic treaty. In that case,

Supply-National Defence I cannot see how we can say that we have any collective strength at all, if we are not prepared to make commitments to those who are our allies.
At this point, I should like to quote a sentence which appears on page 13 of the white paper issued last year. It reads as follows:
There hardly remains an inhabited point on the map too remote to be directly affected.
That refers, of course, to the unhappy tragedy of a war.
Such a conflict, while constituting man's greatest failure to live intelligently with his fellow-men, would also, paradoxically, necessitate a degree of co-operation previously unimagined, among those nations and individuals who value freedom.
Those words are profoundly true. But why do we have to wait until the calamity of a war is upon us before we learn that lesson? Why can we not do these things now, if they are going to add to our defence, as I am convinced they are? Why can we not achieve this degree of co-operation now?
In this document, at page 8, we are told:
By pooling resources, the effect of the pact should be to reduce the total expenditures which each of the 12 countries would have found necessary for their security had there been no pact.
That also is very true. One would think then that, under a system of collective security, the national commitments for each nation would be cut down accordingly, because our strength would be the strength of the entire group. To have the sort of co-operation which is envisaged in the white paper when war comes, demands the surrender of certain powers to a supranational authority. I am more than willing to see that done now, rather than wait until a war comes upon us-if indeed one does come. If we wish to make the North Atlantic treaty a reality, then certain powers have to be surrendered to a supranational authority. The trend has to be towards the nucleus of an international army among those powers.
There are other questions which I should like to ask the minister, and to which he may reply later, concerning matters which were not touched upon by the member for Nanaimo. What is the industrial defence board doing now? Under the order in council which constituted it, it was asked to prepare, and keep up to date, a plan for industrial production in the event of war. I should like to know how far that plan has gone, and if the plan is being kept up to date. Then, the industrial defence board was asked to advise on the locations of industry. What sort of advice is it giving? Obviously, under the conditions which prevail in the world today, if there were to be a war, then decentralization


of industry would be highly advisable. Are any plans being made for such decentralization?
The industrial defence board was asked to advise on the maintenance of reserve stocks. What is the situation with regard to our stockpiling of chrome, manganese, tin, and natural rubber? I do not ask that details be given to the house, but I think some total figure in terms of dollars might be given to us, so that we should have some appreciation at least of what is being done.
The Canadian Commercial Corporation apparently was asked to try to place shadow contracts with various industries throughout the country, to ascertain if requirements could be met in case of necessity. I should be interested in knowing if this has happened, and what the result has been of placing such shadow contracts. In a speech which the minister made about a year and a half ago now, I think to the Canadian Ordnance Association in Montreal, he commented upon the position of the steel industry in Canada. He emphasized the tremendous importance of steel to our economy. We still produce far less than our requirements. I should like to know if the government is preparing for the worst. Obviously, this department should be one which, while it hopes for the best, should nevertheless prepare for the worst. I would like to know what the policy of the department is with regard to this industry. If Canada is not producing sufficient steel for her needs, if she is dependent on other nations, might it not be advisable to carry out policies which would ensure the steel Canada needs? Would there be any better way of doing it-in fact it would be killing two birds with one stone-than by rehabilitating the maritimes by building an efficient steel industry down there? It could only be done by the government taking over that corporation which is known as Dosco.
There was another matter which was not referred to by the minister, the question of defence research. I imagine this is one of the most important departments under the minister. It is spending less money this year than it spent last year, although the supplementary estimates may increase the amount. Nevertheless here is a department which is surely a key to many of the things we want to find out; and we are justified in asking what sort of security clearance is used in this department. I think hon. members may know by now I am not one of those who are enthusiastic about security clearance, but I realize the necessity for it. I ask the question from the point of view of United States experience, where able and competent young scientists

have volunteered their services to government bureaux only to And that the interminable delay of security clearance was such that they got fed up and, instead of working for the country, devoted their talents elsewhere. Are we short of skilled and trained staff in the defence research department? Have we all the men we need? Are we giving those who are there the opportunity of productive work?
I think the most important point I want to make, and one which I think the minister should answer because there may be an answer to it, is this apparent illogicality of his, as I call it, where he talks about the best guarantee of strength being collective security, and then states that we have made no specific commitments under the treaty. I do not think that Canadians would have any objections at all to specific commitments under the .treaty; and we in parliament certainly would want to know what they are. Most certainly I am convinced that there can be no collective strength until we have given these specific commitments to those who shall be our allies.

I am glad the Minister of National Defence is here, Mr. Chairman. I should like to bring some facts before the committee. I have been interested in listening to what has been said by the minister, by the hon. member for Nanaimo and the other members who have spoken. I am not familiar with logistics, but I have received many letters from soldiers and men who want to get into the army, and I should like to explain their case.
Over the C.B.C. there is a program called "Comrades in Arms"; in French, it is "Tambour Battant", beating the drum. It is supposed to help recruiting, and it is wonderful. There are Mexican songs and tom-tom and all sorts of tunes that are supposed to invite young men in good health to join the colours; and it must be quite expensive. It has been running for some time. I do not listen to it regularly, but I hear it occasionally. There is always the same announcement at the beginning and at the end. There are no military marches and there is no military inspiration in the music that we hear. It is just fun, Viennese waltzes and other things. It is quite astonishing.
I have a case that I am going to mention to the minister. He must be familiar with it because we had some correspondence about it. I am unfolding some of the files to which I referred the other day on another matter. The case I refer to now is that of Romeo Santerre, who is a nice fellow, less than 25 years of age, with three years' service in the army, of which one and a half years was
Supply-National Defence overseas. He was honourably discharged and now he would like to get into the army. In spite of "Comrades in Arms" and "Tambour Battant", beating the drum, I am obliged to fight for him in order to get him into the army.
What to me seems stupid on the part of the brass hats is their paying for a program over the radio to invite young men to get into the army and then failing to accept them when they are able-bodied and willing to come in. I have this man's regimental number here. I will give it to the brass hats who probably adorn the gallery. I do not know whether there are any there. I find the brass hats stupid. The number is E-100850. The reason the young man is not accepted by the army is that he has not sufficient education to meet their standards. Who ever heard of such a thing? He must be a B.A. in order to be accepted in the army! What is the use of having a program over the radio, in both languages, telling young men "join up", "get into the army", "you will be happy in the army", "there is a career for you in the army"? Romeo Santerre listened to that in French and said to himself, "That is my chance to get a job. I have been in the army. I have nothing to do. I am unemployed. I am ready to go back again. Although I saw many things in the army that were unpleasant I do not mind about that; I am ready to go; I am willing to go. I have my experience of one and a half years overseas and one and a half years here in Canada. I think I am fit. I was honourably discharged. I want to join the colours." If that man joined the colours after having listened to the program, we would think the program was worth something, having regard to the money expended on it.
Romeo Santerre tries to join the army. Is he accepted? No, sir; he is not accepted because he is not highly enough educated. He must be a B.A. He must go to a university. He must be like the civil servants. The army seems to be like the civil service. In the civil service a man must have university degrees in order to get irj. They must have a gilt embossed parchment attesting the degree of M.Sc. and then they are doctors; they wear mortarboards. What the army wants is not able-bodied men; it is men with mortarboards. The army is just the same as the civil service commission. I am quite indignant about this matter. Here is a young man who is willing to go into the army. But can he get in? No, sir. They say to him, "You have no mortarboard; you have no honorary degree, you have no degree of doctor of laws from a university that did not give you any lectures on law; you are

Prairie Transmission Lines not qualified to get into the army. You are too ignorant." Who ever heard of such a thing?

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed, from Friday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benidick-son for the second reading of Bill No. 9, to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, and the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Edmonton East): "That this question be now ' put."
Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker,
I had not intended to speak on this pipe lines bill, and I do not wish to delay proceedings unduly. However, the hon. member who preceded me in the debate, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), made certain remarks with which I think I should deal.
In his speech on March 14, reported in Hansard at page 748, he said:
May I warn members from some of the other provinces. Let us first take those from Saskatchewan. They may find the next step will be that instead of their towns being supplied with natural gas that gas will be sent down into the United States.
Then he proceeded to warn members from Quebec and, finally, to chastise the four Liberal members from British Columbia, implying that these members were not doing their duty by their own province, and that they had favoured the bill-although, as has been pointed out, all they did was to move for a vote.
Before I received the advice from the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, I had communicated with the province of Saskatchewan. The city of Yorkton, in which I am particularly interested, is not, I think, very much concerned with the bill, because in that constituency at the town of Kamsack we have found gas, and it is now being partially supplied with gas.
In any event we are interested as a province; and with that in mind before the hon. member spoke I had communicated with the

boards of trade in Saskatoon and Regina as to what action if any they wanted the Saskatchewan members to take with regard to these bills which, as hon. members know, were debated in the last session, as well as in this one.
In that connection I also asked a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), which is reported in Hansard at page 792 as follows:
Have any representations been made to him by the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan with regard to protecting Saskatchewan so far as the export of oil and gas from Alberta is concerned?
In reply to that the minister answered in these words:
I have no knowledge of any representations from the province of Saskatchewan in that connection.
My second question was:
What is the policy of the minister with regard to the granting of permits for pipe lines from Alberta
to the United States?
In answer to my second question he said:
I would say that I spoke on this subject at the last session of parliament, and pointed out that the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act is designed to protect Canadian consumers. It is necessary under the act for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to give a certificate to the effect that the present and foreable future needs of Canada are protected before any exports of electricity or gas are permitted. It has been suggested frequently in the current debate that gas will be sent to the United States from the pipe line before the pipe line reaches Vancouver. I stated last session that that would not be permitted. I know from discussions with the sponsors of the pipe line that it is not proposed to undertake any such export.
Iii addition I have received a copy of a letter which the commissioner and the board of trade of Saskatoon sent to the Hon. J. H. Broekelbank, minister of rtatural resources and industrial development in Saskatchewan, at Regina, dated March 13. That letter points out that it has been brought to their attention that a private bill was coming before the house in connection with this matter.
The question was raised as to whether Saskatchewan's interests in getting a supply of gas should not be protected. The thought was that in any such bill authorizing the exportation of gas to centres in British Columbia Saskatchewan's probable needs of natural gas should be provided for, before any gas was exported to British Columbia.
With that I agree. I have checked the history of these pipe line bills that were passed at a session of parliament before many hon. members who now hold a seat were here. I refer to the session in April of 1949. Apparently all these bills received second reading on April 29 of that year.
I was interested to note what the sponsors of the attack on the present bill had done

to safeguard the interests of Saskatchewan in connection with the previous legislation. I find they took no stand on it at all. Bill C-8 was not passed, and that was an application from this same company. Then I find that on April 29, 1949, Bill B-8 was passed, under which the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company obtained a charter in the same wording as the application in the present instance, giving them rights within or outside Canada.
Then I find that the Trans-Northern Pipe Line Company, oil only, also obtained a charter, with rights within or outside Canada. I find, further, that the British American Pipe Line Company on the same date from the House of Commons obtained a charter, for oil only, within and outside Canada.
Then I find a bill, sponsored I believe by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), for the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. It was passed, but it only gives permission within Alberta and British Columbia, or outside Canada, to construct a pipe line for gas and oil. So that in that bill Saskatchewan is left in the choice position of not having any interest at all. They got a charter for the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. By that bill Saskatchewan was left in the cold.
The bill now before the house proceeds to follow exactly the same language in which the other bills were passed, and those bills were not questioned. No riders were added and no amendments moved either by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra or the hon. member tor Fraser Valley in any way limiting the route of the pipe line, or anything of that nature. I have checked that.
Has the hon. member checked the proceedings before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines? If he does he will find that that was where we got that pledge.

I am taking the record of Hansard. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is quite a skilful lawyer, but I do not think he will attempt to convey to this house that anything said before a committee is binding when there is nothing in the bill. With his legal experience I doubt if he will contend that for one second. The previous bill passed without any amendment. I think the hon. member will agree that anything said before a committee of this house is not binding or operative on anyone.

Unless the people behind this company are entirely dishonest, the pledge they gave before that committee would bind them.
Prairie Transmission Lines

The hon. member who sponsors this bill, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), is reported on page 447 of Hansard of March 3, 1950, when replying to a question by one of the opponents of the bill, as saying:
I have given the assurance. Mr. Speaker, that this company is quite prepared to build a pipe line wherever any of these regulatory bodies insist that it be built.
That is a much more binding undertaking given before the whole house than anything that might be given before a committee. The same hon. member pointed out during the debate that the Alberta government is not opposed to the incorporation of the particular company provided for in this bill. On the contrary, that government feels strongly that no bona fide company should be refused incorporation and thus deprive and limit the province of Alberta from dealing with several companies instead of one. The leader of the Social Credit group also made it quite clear that he wanted a vote on this bill on its merits and also wanted it referred to a committee of the house.
I repeat that the bill that passed the house covers only the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia-Saskatchewan was completely out in the cold. Should this bill pass permission will be given to incorporate a company that can operate in Saskatchewan. It looks to me very much as though there were a nigger in the woodpile. The same hon. gentlemen are now strenuously opposing the granting of a charter to a company which the government of Alberta is in favour of.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave an opinion which I concur in with deference- I submit the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) concurred in it also-that the province of Alberta alone has jurisdiction over the oil in Alberta while it is in Alberta. In addition conservation measures were prepared by the hon. member for Calgary West, according to his statement-we will presume that with his usual thoroughness he included every protection necessary for the province of Alberta-and they provide that the conservation board must ratify and give consent to the exportation of oil or gas from Alberta. Until they do that neither the company that has been formed nor the company that is proposed by this bill will be able to build a pipe line to move gas or oil out of the province of Alberta.
Then in addition the province of Alberta has safeguarded itself further in connection with how much oil or gas shall be exported from the province. They have ruled, and properly so, that the people of Alberta must come first and then the other provinces and the United States. The hon. member for

I disagree entirely with my hon. friend.
The hon. member is not reported in Hansard. He will have an opportunity later in this debate to produce Hansard.

I intend to be on

Which would cost more, a pipe line to Saskatchewan or a pipe line to British Columbia?

Because of the mountains, a pipe line to British Columbia would naturally cost more than one to Saskatchewan. We have some splendid cities in that province, including Saskatoon, Moose Jaw and Regina, and I am not forgetting my own city of Yorkton. my contention that the province of Alberta has the whole say as to whether a pipe line is built for the purpose of exporting oil from that province. The same thing applies to Quebec. Oh.

I concede that, and distinctly more than you do.

I should like to quote from page 2651 of Hansard of April 27, 1949, where the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
I do not think the parliament of Canada would have the right to say to those operating on crown lands in the province of Quebec. "You shall have the right to export wood cut on those crown lands." That wood is simply not exportable. I would imagine it might be the same situation with respect to gas taken from concessions in any other province. I would imagine the province would have the right to say, "We will allow you to exploit these lands provided you do not send the product from these lands outside of Canada."
As Alberta has the right to do. The Prime Minister continued:
In that case I do not think any licence granted under federal authority would authorize a concessionaire to export contrary to the conditions of his concession from the owners, that is to say, the provincial government.

That is a term of the contract.
He apparently agreed with the Prime Minister.

speechtext:
A term of the contract, and I
do not think, whatever be the terms ef the federal legislation with respect to permits, that such a permit could give one holding a concession the right to violate his contract.
In other words, any company will first have to enter into a contract with the government of the province of Alberta, and no doubt that government will make sure that the contract is fair not only to Alberta but also to the other provinces of Canada. right to violate his contract. It might very well be that, although the owner under the contract did not forbid exportation-
The province of Alberta is the owner of 90 per cent of their oil and gas and they likely would forbid export.

Or to cross a boundary.

speechtext: I am sorry, it does not.

In spite of what the hon. member has just said, the legislature of the province of Quebec has made pulpwood, which is a product of the forests, non-exportable from Canada in an unmanufactured state. That has been going on for over thirty years and the law has been respected and followed, and is valid legislation. Therefore I say that, in so far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, I am in favour of the bill being given second reading and going before a committee of the house. I am most surprised that members of the C.C.F. are opposing the government of the province of Alberta which wants the bill passed. They want competition. If you leave the situation as it is with only one measure incorporating a company on the statute books you are creating a monopoly. You are allowing only one company to have a charter. It is far more favourable to the people of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to have several companies competing with each other. We will get cheaper gas and oil, but if you give a monopoly to one, as was done in April of 1949 without the C.C.F. saying one word against it, without even moving an amendment, you are simply building up a monopoly, and you have done that in the province of Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Yorkton, who has just

concluded his remarks, has made some statements which I think require to be dealt with immediately. I should like to deal with the last one first. He said that if no further companies are permitted incorporation before this house we will be creating a monopoly. It is not this house which will be creating a monopoly. The very nature of the gas pipe line industry itself creates a monopoly. For that and similar reasons the Alberta government has set up its gas conservation board and the British Columbia government has set up its public utilities commission. The two provinces have similar legislation to control the price to be charged for those products or utilities which are in the nature of monopolies. So the fact that there may be two or three companies seeking incorporation, or that two or three companies may be incorporated, would not make the slightest difference to the price of gas in Alberta or British Columbia, in that set-up.
So the issue before us, and the only issue, is whether or not we shall incorporate a company which has declared that it intends to build its line through the United States. It is on that issue that we as members of this house are asked to make up our minds in voting for or against this bill. Before I go on to deal with that point in detail may I refer to two or three other arguments advanced by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart). He has referred to the fact that last year we incorporated a number of companies. At least two if not three of the companies he mentioned had to do with oil pipe lines. The Interprovincial and the B-A are certainly oil pipe lines; and an oil pipe line has nothing in common with a gas pipe line. What is before us tonight is a bill to incorporate a company to build a gas pipe line. An oil pipe line is a common carrier. The oil must be taken to a refinery and processed before it is of any use. Gas, however, is available as soon as you put in a branch or distributing line and tap the main pipe line. You have a commodity in a form in which it can be used right away. So there is no comparison between the two undertakings; and the fact that last year we incorporated oil pipe-line companies is no argument in favour of continuing to incorporate gas pipe-line companies.
Let me say further that while we incorporated the Westcoast company last year to convey gas, when it was realized that there was before the house no undertaking from the company as to whether or not they would serve Canada first, the company was asked in committee-which was the only available place at that time where they could be asked -whether they would build their line through Canada or where they intended to build it;

and as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has pointed out, they gave a firm undertaking to build their line through Canada. Since that time they have been before the Alberta board asking permission to export gas over a Canadian route which they have laid down in black and white.
Is that line not for gas or oil?
Gas.
Look at your statute.
I am referring to the application made by the company to the Alberta board.
I would point out to the hon. member that the Westcoast company has to do with gas and oil.

The proposal was to construct a gas pipe line. There are certain considerations which must be borne in mind by hon. members when dealing with this bill, considerations of national as well as local policy. May I deal first with the considerations of local policy. I would inform the house that yesterday the British Columbia legislature passed unanimously a resolution asking that the pipe line from the Alberta gas fields to the Pacific coast should be built through Canada.

Would the hon. member permit a question on that? Am I not correct in saying that in the coalition government of British Columbia there are both Liberals and Conservatives, and that it was also endorsed by the C.C.F.?
That statement is correct.
Did British Columbia also ask that we should not pass this bill?

I shall read the resolution which was adopted unanimously by the British Columbia legislature yesterday. It was introduced by Mr. G. E. Braden, M.L.A. for Peace River:
Whereas there are strong indications that a great potential of both petroleum and natural gas exists in the northeastern section of British Columbia:
And whereas exploration is presently taking place to ascertain the extent and value of these resources:
And whereas it would be a further incentive to greater and more intensive exploration if an outlet to market of these commodities was available:
And whereas proposals are now being considered for the construction of gas and petroleum pipe lines from available supplies in Alberta to Vancouver and the Pacific coast states of the United States:
And referring to the last question of the hon. member for Yorkton, I might say that those words-
Prairie Transmission Lines
Read it.

Obviously those words refer to the proposals now before this house. The resolution continues:
And whereas, in the opinion of many members of this legislature the requirements of Canadians in this connection would be a matter of first consideration:
And whereas the industrial development of the interior of British Columba as well as the Vancouver and Fraser valley areas would be greatly stimulated by the construction of oil and natural gas pipe lines from Alberta and northeastern British Columbia through the interior of British Columbia to the Pacific coast:
And whereas, if the proposed northern route is followed, many millions of dollars will be spent in British Columbia in the construction of the lines with consequent employment of thousands of our citizens:
Therefore be it resolved, that the legislative assembly of the province of British Columbia urge upon the federal and provincial authorities concerned the advisability in the interests not only of British Columbia but of Canada as well that such pipe lines be constructed through the Yellowhead pass and thence through the interior of British Columbia to Vancouver, with provision for the extension of the line to the Peace river block so that when sufficient supplies of petroleum and natural gas are available in that area there will be an available outlet to market without unnecessary delay.
Now would the hon. member permit another question on that, just to make it clear? That was adopted by all parties, was it not?
That resolution was adopted, as the hon. member said, by all parties in the British Columbia house.
And they did not oppose this bill.

As hon, members of this house know, at the present time there is a coalition government in British Columbia made up of Liberal and Conservative members, the opposition being the C.C.F.; and every member in the house subscribed to this resolution. It asks in specific terms that the route of the proposed pipe line from Alberta to the Pacific coast be through the Yellowhead pass and into British Columbia. That is the route proposed to be followed by the Westcoast Transmission Company; and so far that company alone has given the assurance that this route will be followed. Speaking for myself- though if I have been able to follow the arguments of others who have spoken I think I can speak for them as well-if any other company seeking incorporation will give a similar undertaking that it will follow this route to British Columbia, then I will withdraw my objection to its bill.
I am basing my stand and my appeal to the members of this house tonight on what this
876

Prairie Transmission Lines pipe line, if it is built through British Columbia, will mean to the area I come from, to my province, and to this country, and what it will mean to have the principle accepted that pipe lines transporting Canadian resources should serve Canada first.
May I just remind hon. members of the two alternatives placed before the house by the member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), in his very able speech the other day. He placed before us the two alternatives we have in considering these bills. On the one hand, there is the possibility of a route through Canada, serving the Canadian cities en route, and providing adequate natural gas for those cities, as far as we know forever, and certainly for the foreseeable future. That route from Alberta to the Pacific coast, if it is built through Canada, will not only supply the Vancouver and Pacific coast market, but it will serve the Canadian cities in the interior of British Columbia through which it passes. And such a pipe line, Mr. Speaker, will serve the Pacific coast market, including the United States cities on the Pacific coast, just as well if it is built through the interior of British Columbia, as it will if the route is down through the United States. So there is no question of any member who has spoken in opposition to this bill seeking to deny export of gas to the United States. There will be as much gas exported to the United States through that Yellowhead route as there will be through the U.S. route these companies are asking for. Our point is that we want the route to go through Canada first, and serve the Canadian cities en route.

Will the hon. member permit one more question? Do you agree with the statement made by the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) before the Gyro club in the city of Ottawa? This is the statement:
. . . oil and gas are found together and so abundant is the latter that "enough gas to supply the needs of Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and all eastern Canada is being wasted in flares. If we had a market for our gas, we could continue our search for oil," said the speaker in conclusion.
We are trying to get a market for it.
We want the pipe line routed through Canada.

If the hon. gentleman would open his mind, instead of closing it, he would realize that we are all equally ready to serve Alberta, and help find a market, but we want the pipe line routed to its market through Canada instead of the United States. We have one proposition, a route to the Pacific coast' of the United States through Canada, and serving the Canadian cities and towns

en route. We have the other alternative of a route proposed by this company whose bill is before us tonight, the major portion of which would run through the United States. It would serve the same ultimate market on the Pacific coast, without any similar advantages to Canada. There would be no advantage to Canada, either in its construction, because it will be built through the United States, or in its maintenance, because it will lie in the United States. There will be no service to the Canadian cities in the interior of the province of British Columbia, which would be served by the other route.
Why is it there are only these two alternatives? Why is it that if the route to the Pacific coast is through the United States the interior of British Columbia will not be served? The answer is, and again I am quoting, amongst others, the authority of the member for Calgary West, upon whose statements the member for Yorkton seems to place a good deal of reliance, that there will be only one pipe line from Alberta to the Pacific coast. If hon. members will reflect, they will see that is the case. The significance of that factor is, and I think it must be admitted, that the market in the interior of British Columbia, Kamloops, Vernon, Kelowna and Penticton-those interior cities- is not large enough to warrant a separate pipe line being built to serve that market alone. If, therefore, that line goes to Vancouver and the Pacific coast via the United States and does not go through our area, we will not get a pipe line built back up from the coast to serve us. If the line goes by any other route, we will not be served with gas. If it is built through our area, then it is a simple matter-I have talked with the officials of the company-to serve the cities along that route.
Furthermore, a definite assurance has been given that the company will service these cities, and will service the whole of the Okanagan area as well. I ask hon. members to consider the area which is vitally concerned in this matter. There are the four large centres I have mentioned, Kamloops, Vernon, Kelowna, Penticton, all cities of between ten and fifteen thousand people. Each one serves a tremendous area of its own. The other cities farther to the south, Oliver and Osoyoos, and the Merritt, Princeton and Hope districts will be served as well. To put a conservative estimate on it, that area contains at least 100,000 to 150,000 people. If this pipe line follows the route to the United States, that area will not be served with gas. You can see, Mr. Speaker, what it means to have the pipe line built through the interior of British Columbia.

To answer the question which the hon. member has asked me, I have talked this matter over with the officials of the Westcoast Transmission Company-
Oh, oh.

-who assure me that the problem of supplying cities such as Kamloops, Kelowna and Penticton with natural gas on the route of the pipe line is a problem which they are well qualified to handle, and one which they are prepared and anxious to undertake. They have looked into the matter, and have satisfied themselves it will be
Prairie Transmission Lines economically desirable for them to supply that market if their pipe line goes through that area.
Then, dealing with the question of the views of the people whom I represent, I should like to read some of the resolutions which have been sent to me in support of the Canadian route. On February 13, the Kamloops board of trade passed a resolution which reads as follows:
Whereas it is the opinion of this Kamloops board of trade that Canada's natural resources should be used to serve Canada first and to promote the welfare and growth of the Canadian economy before being exported;
and whereas there is need' of a conscious and dynamic policy to develop Canada's resources and economy;
therefore be it resolved that with respect to the construction of a gas pipe line to serve Pacific coast cities using Alberta natural gas this Kamloops board of trade is of opinion that the route of such pipe line should be built so far as possible through Canadian territory first so as to serve Canadian cities before the gas is exported to the United States.
At their meeting last Sunday in Revelstoke, the Mainline-Okanagan associated boards of trade endorsed that resolution according to a wire I received today; and that association represents the main line boards of trade from Chilliwack to Revelstoke and the Okanagan boards of trade from the areas of Vernon, Kelowna and Penticton, all those areas being unanimous in support of the resolution.
I have similar letters or resolutions from the Kamloops junior chamber of commerce, the Osoyoos junior chamber of commerce, the Penticton junior chamber of commerce, the Smithers junior chamber of commerce, the Vernon junior chamber of commerce-
Do any of these resolutions oppose this bill?

-the central north Thompson board of trade, the Blue river and district board of trade and the Rutland board of trade. Those are only some of the resolutions and telegrams which hon. members from the interior of British Columbia have been receiving in connection with this matter.
And the Fraser valley.

In our desire to obtain the services of a cheap source of power, which we will obtain only if this pipe line is routed through British Columbia, we in the interior of the province face a problem which is very much the same as the over-all problem as between Canada and the enormously more powerful industrial nation of the United States, which brings me to a consideration of the wider implications of this measure and what I consider should be a national policy for the use of Canada's resources. As in all areas which are not yet fully developed and

Prairie Transmission Lines industrialized, we in the interior of British Columbia are at a disadvantage as compared with the more heavily industrialized centres of the country. Whenever you go to an industry and try to attract it to such areas as that, the answer is that they are too far from the markets and that they are too far from cheap sources of power to make it economically wise to build their industry in that area; hence we go around in what sometimes amounts to a sort of vicious circle. Because the sources of power and the markets already exist, let us say at the coast, the industry goes down and establishes there. This action increases the market, it increases the facilities and increases the disproportion between the undeveloped and the developed areas. I am speaking here from the point of view of local interest. That is why we want this gas in the interior of British Columbia, and we can have it without doing any disservice to the coastal areas; because it is as advantageous to build through our district, and the supplies of gas are ample to supply us and still leave plenty over for Vancouver, the other Pacific coast cities, and the United States.
In that respect there is a parallel between our position vis-a-vis the already developed coastal areas and the position of Canada in comparison with the United States. If we allow this gas to go to the United States Pacific coast cities before it goes to Vancouver, the result is obvious. Vancouver will be at the end of a branch line. Vancouver's gas will cost more than the gas in the United States cities which will be served first. The United States is already more highly industrialized than is Canada. Because the gas will be served to them at a cheaper rate, it will be more attractive for industry to go to the United States, and hence the disproportion between Canada's industrial development and that of the United States will be perpetuated if the route should be built through the United States first.
That brings me to the broad national question of the policy of building Canada first, the policy which is actually inherent in this gas pipe-line bill and in the stand of those who are opposed to the incorporation of a company which does not give us the assurance that it will build its route through Canada. If the various governments of Canada had never taken the stand that Canada's resources should be developed for Canada first and that they were going to build a nation here north of the forty-ninth parallel, we would never have reached even the stage of development that we have today. One has only to think back to the history of the construction of our railways to realize

that it is only when governments and parliaments assume their full responsibility with respect to the directing of the national policy that we can have national growth along conscious and positive lines.
Mr. Speaker, it is nine o'clock, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

It being nine o'clock, the house will resume the business that was interrupted at six o'clock.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE Defence forces-
202. To provide for the defence forces of the navy, army and air services, and to authorize total commitments for this purpose of $579,301,670 including authority, notwithstanding section 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, to make commitments for the current year of $438,178,000 and commitments for future years of $141,123,670 against which commitments it is estimated that actual expenditures in 1950-51 will not exceed $384,932,304.

I wish to continue, Mr. Chairman, with what I was saying before the dinner recess. I was complaining of the silly program called "Comrades in Arms" or "Tambour Battant", which is pure nonsense. I was going to ask the minister, as he is familiar with the case of Romeo Santerre, if he would have any objection to taking him into the army again. This is my question, and the reason is obvious. He had something more and something much better than any university degree. He had experience in a theatre of war to the extent of several months. As I wrote on December 21 last, the experience that he has acquired on the battlefield should be a greater asset than any university education. May I ask the minister if he will take him into the army again.

I shall be glad indeed to take into consideration the representations made by the hon. member, but I cannot guarantee that the candidate for service in the armed forces would conform to our requirements at the time. I shall be glad, however, to look into the matter again.

I thank the minister, but I will ask him to be kind enough to tell me something about the requirements for getting into the armed forces. It seems to me that the radio listener should be warned that applicants must have mortarboards before they can be admitted to the army. It is not fair to say to them, "Come in; come in", if they are not all accepted. Instead of the silly prologue to that broadcast a warning should

be given to all those who have not enough education, according to the standards established by the Department of National Defence. The program should be known as one to invite people not to enlist, instead of one calling them to the colours.
This is something absolutely nonsensical. Why should a country pay for that program if it serves no purpose, and if those who are willing to enlist are refused the opportunity, particularly when they show what Mr. King would have called good will? That is something beyond my understanding. I do not understand it at all.
I would ask the minister to be good enough to give us the titles of the songs on the program, the titles of the musical parts, both in French and in English, since their beginning. We will see that we will have Strauss and all the other Viennese composers coming to the fore to call people to the colours. Well, if so, it will be quite unusual. I want to know, further, how much this cost the country, and what the results were. In the case of Romeo Santerre they were nil. I am wondering if they have been better for others.
It may be that other fellows who were qualified to be good soldiers, who had good eyesight so that they could shoot straight, and who were able-bodied, have been refused, perhaps because they could not write Latin verse, or because they could not make a translation from French into Greek.
It is the funniest thing; in virtue of the North Atlantic pact, I was under the impression that these things had been decided, and that the examples I have given must have been due to the eccentricities of someone from Oxford or Cambridge, or from some French lycee who wished to show his importance in the drafting of a program like that.
What are the important qualifications of a soldier? He must have sufficient intelligence to understand orders given to him by his commanding officer; he must have good health and good training. I appeal to all those who have been in the army, I appeal to the minister and to his critic, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), and ask them bluntly if the best soldiers they had under them were not precisely lumberjacks who, perhaps, could not read or write, but who were always on the job. They were the best shots, the best marksmen. They were able to walk long distances and were physically trained to be soldiers.
Those men were not university graduates- far from it. They were the ones who went to war under the command of experienced officers such as the hon. member for Nanaimo, and others.

Hear, hear.
Supply-National Defence

I thank hon. members who are returned men for their approval. They were fortunate enough to have education, but they did not turn a cold shoulder to the men who were the backbone of the army, and who were always there when there was a difficult task to accomplish. That is that.
We are in an age of super-education. We are in an age of mortarboards and gowns. We are in an age where people are much too clever. That is why Romeo Santerre was not accepted when he wanted to enlist again as a private. Incredible! I know Romeo Santerre well. He is a nice, clean fellow.
A good man in a tight corner.

Yes, a straight, first-class man for the army. I would not recommend him as secretary to my hon. friend, or as chief of staff in the Department of National Defence; but I do recommend him as a private soldier. He wants to be a private soldier, and I want him to be.
I am for the voluntary system; I am not for conscription. During the last war the government sent military police to look after the farmers' sons and to take them to the clink. I believed the farmers were needed on the farms, and objected to the action then taken. I was for voluntary service, and when a young man wants to enlist I do not see why those who call for recruiting should object to it. That is why I am so insistent upon having this man accepted in the army. I guarantee to the minister that he will* be a good soldier.
I have another case to put before the minister, and this one refers to a young man with more education than the first one I mentioned. He is a fine fellow, but was not accepted in the R.C.A.F. because he had a year less in education than was required for the training. A notice was sent to him in French, and I see in that letter some mistakes in French grammar. The letter was sent by the commanding officer of the Quebec station. I say that officer should first learn French grammar, before he is in a position to tell others to be well educated. It is absurd!
There are other cases. I have many others, but I brought only a few with me to the chamber. The one I shall now mention concerns a cook who would like to join the army to serve in the kitchen and to prepare good meals. This man is a good cook, but he suffers a little from his feet. I understand that a cook is not required to be a professor of gymnastics; he has other things to do than playing the role of acrobat in the army. Because this man has sore feet he is not to be admitted. There are obstacles in the way all the time.

Supply-National Defence
I place before the house another case concerning a man whose name I shall not give, but who is at present in jail. This man would like to be in the army and his case is before the parliamentary assistant. He is in jail because he made a mistake, but that should be forgotten. He is a good marksman and would be able to kill the enemy. If there is a war he is the one I would recommend because he would not miss his mark.
Is that what he is in jail for?

In war everything is permitted. I am relating these stories to indicate that I am not alone in having some good will, as Mr. King would say. There are many others who have good will and who are ready to enlist in the army, but they cannot. Probably when this fellow was in jail the radio of the keeper was on full blast and he heard the famous programs, "Comrades in Arms" and "Tambour Battant". He then said to himself, "This is my chance to get into the army; it is a fine place for me and I am ready to go." Perhaps that was the result of the fine programs in English and French that are heard over C.B.C. at times.
I shall try to summarize these cases as much as I can. During the first days of the war I offered to raise a regiment in my county in one week for the defence of Canada, but my offer was turned down. I never thought that I would be again insisting that the wishes of those who wanted to get into the army should be fulfilled. But, the fact is that many of these men are born warriors.
Then a word about the reserve army. Many of the officers connected with this organization consider themselves very important. Probably they never saw a German or a Jap or any one of our enemies during the last war except from a distance when they were brought here as prisoners. Nevertheless they consider themselves to be important people. I have a letter here about the way cadet officers in the reserve army were dealt with. There was a Captain Schooley, the chief instructor, and a Lieutenant Ravel. I do not know if he is French or Huguenot, but he did not seem to recognize the French language in the camp. Captain Schooley said many times in the class that French was not a handicap to the men speaking that language; it only meant that they had to study three or four times as hard.
The lectures and examinations were all in English. No one spoke French. All the officers were strong personalities and they established an atmosphere in which it was not good for French-speaking people to live. This certainly was less attractive than the

broadcasts "Comrades in Arms" and "Tambour Battant." They were much more interesting.
I mention these things because I think it is positively unfair to invite a person to come to you and then close the door when he arrives. It is not even good manners. I want to bring these facts before the committee in the presence of the minister. The minister must not take it for granted that the brass hats in his department are infallible. I knew most of them during the war and I found them to be as stupid as stones. You could not get anything out of them. They were born stupid. Probably they had a fine education, but no one could see what benefit they got from them. I have never been in the army, but I certainly used the language of the buck private with regard to the high-ups.
That is why we like you.

1 appreciate that remark. It does my heart good to hear remarks like that when I say something that I dislike to say. We are not going to be bossed indefinitely by these brass hats. It is nonsense to ever think of that. A great many of them are still there. We won the first world war, we won the second world war, and they were there in their swivel chairs. During the war we heard much about the importance of swivel chairs. They were going from hemisphere to hemisphere in their swivel chairs.
Around and around.

They were rolling around. I do not want to take up too much time, and besides my time is limited. Yesterday a return was tabled dealing with a private who had been accepted in the army and placed in category A. That meant that his health was good, that he was well, that he was ablebodied, that he was physically qualified to be a good soldier. When he was discharged his Pulhem test P dropped from 1 to 3; M dropped from 2 to 4; S dropped from 1 to 4. This man was well when he was taken into the army but he was no longer well when he came out. It was evident that he suffered disabilities during his service. He was accepted as being in category A, in good health, but when he was discharged his papers indicated that he was no longer well.
Why not be generous and give this man a pension? The minister may say that this matter does not come under the Department of National Defence, but that department was responsible for the medical examination in the first place. He was examined by army doctors, not by doctors of the Department of Veterans Affairs. That man was not on pension when he was examined for the first time. He was entering the army. He was

accepted in the army as a man who was fit. Then he had some service, and when he was discharged he was not at all in the same condition of health as when he entered. When it is established in that manner that that man has suffered a disability of any kind, the presumption is that it was due unquestionably to his military service, but we are told that the disability from which he suffers existed before his enlistment or occurred after his discharge. No pension is paid to him.
I complain in the most severe language against the pension commissioners, but we must also complain against the army doctors who have not fulfilled their duty. To the new members of the house may I say that during the war I had to fight for the soldiers and against the doctors. I received protests from very high medical authorities, but after I had sent them copies of Hansard, in which statements that were according to the facts showed beyond any doubt that the doctors referred to were incompetent, then they said: We never thought that it was as bad as that.
I hope that these people will receive justice, and that justice will not be denied them because the departments concerned refuse to acknowledge the fallibility of certain doctors. I will have other opportunities to speak about this matter. I can tell the minister that some of the cases I have mentioned have amusing aspects superficially, but if we consider them seriously we will realize it is a pity that there are such obstacles in the way of patriotic young men who desire to serve their country, who are qualified to accomplish that noble duty, and who cannot do so on account of the stupidity and procrastination of some important bigwigs in the Department of National Defence. In my humble view it is time to stop it. After the sitting this afternoon I met many of my colleagues who told me that I was perfectly right, and that they realized the difficulties young men have to get into the army, especially if they are from the province of Quebec. As I am an advocate of voluntary service, I hope that those who are willing to enter the army will have no obstacles placed in their way, and will be admitted as the good Canadians that they are.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I shall not be able to bring to you the technical skill that the hon. member for Nanaimo did this afternoon nor the sprightly personalities with which the hon. member for Temiscouata has just delighted us. I certainly agree with him that I would much rather have a good cook with bad feet than a bad cook with good feet. Indeed, it seems to me there might be some possible advantage in having a cook whose feet were not too good because it might keep him beside
Supply-National Defence the stove on his job. I would say to the hon. member, however, that I had a very desolating experience in 1939 which perhaps throws some light on the different qualifications which apparently are now required from soldiers. A friend of mine, who like myself had been in the first war, received a letter from his son who had joined up for the second war. This was in the autumn of 1939, and the letter contained a sentence which was devastating to us. The young man wrote to his father and said: War has now reached the stage where an intelligent man can take part in it. I submit to the hon. member for Temiscouata that possibly that has something to do with the new regulations.
Tonight I propose not to talk about the technique of war, which indeed I am not qualified to do, but to discuss the question of how we in the opposition are to discharge our duty with respect to the expenditure of the huge sums of money that are now being brought before the house by the Minister of National Defence. I listened of course with great interest, as other hon. members did, to his speech this afternoon. Certainly when one thinks that he has been from Alaska as far as Berlin or farther in the course of his duties, it gives us an idea both of the way the world has shrunk and of the way in which our responsibilities have extended. I could not help taking a particular interest in the paymaster who jumped with the men. If he landed in Alaska I hope he had the proper qualifications from the foreign exchange control board before he started out; otherwise he may be in for great difficulties. I must say I sympathize with him in taking those risks merely for the sake of seeing that the men had their money. I would have thought that a little higher degree of organization might have enabled the men to have their money before they started, but maybe he was a sporting fellow and liked to jump.
He landed in Alaska, he brought the money, the men received the money in Alaska in Canadian funds, made their purchases in Canadian funds, and everything was fine.

Oh, I see; you had a sort of extraterritoriality there. At any rate, there it is. I think we agree with the minister that the meetings which he attends, and which produce the personal contacts that he mentioned, are valuable as he says. We find it easy to accept his assurance that our men compare very favourably with any others. When he says that our defence is in better shape than it ever was before in peacetime I think we will say it certainly ought to be, considering the amount we are spending on it.

Supply-National Defence
I feel almost apologetic in bringing the house to the sordid consideration of money and how it is to be spent, but after all that is our duty, and therefore I propose to do so.
I should like to remind the house again of the huge total sum which we are considering, some $579 million, more, if I remember correctly, than our whole expenditure in the last year before the war. I should like to refer the committee particularly to just one of the large lump expenditures that we are facing. I have picked this one out because it is the largest single gobbet that I see, that is to say, $80 million odd in the air force for stores, equipment, aircraft and so on. I mention that just to bring before the committee the astonishing size of the amounts that we are now dealing with.
I go on to ask what is the duty of the government and of the opposition-because after all we are part of the machinery of government in this country-in these circumstances; and I want to read just part of a sentence from a small book by a distinguished British parliamentarian, Quintin Hogg, which is called "The Purpose of Parliament":
It is not the right of the government to stifle criticism; it must, therefore, put down for discussion such financial items as the opposition wish to discuss.
That, of course, refers to the British practice, and I merely want to stress the one word "discuss". It is the matter of discussion I wish to bring to the attention of the committee; and I suggest that you cannot discuss a thing unless you have the necessary information enabling you to do so. It is this question of information which I wish to bat up to the minister, so to speak, tonight.
I want to say a general word about the way this house now deals with the estimates that come before it. If an intelligent citizen observed all the time this house spends in dealing with the estimates and saw what really happens, I think he might very easily come to the conclusion that he had been witnessing a solemn farce; for I doubt if a single member in this house has ever seen a single dollar lopped off a single item. If the hon. member for Quebec South were in his place he would be an exception, because I find that in 1922 he was actually instrumental in having some hundreds of thousands of dollars lopped off the defence estimates, when his own party was in power. But then, of course, the hon. member has qualities and capacities which are denied to us more ordinary people.
What happens now? I think all hon. members will agree that when an estimate comes into this house it is a government measure. We do not discuss it. We ask questions about it, but. we do not discuss it. What Quintin Hogg says should happen does not happen,
(Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
because when you discuss a thing presumably it is with the idea that something is going to be done about it. Since I have been in this house, as far as I can remember, not a dollar has ever been cut off any estimate that has come up. Everything brought in here is a government measure. Indeed, it is more than that; the ingenious Minister of Trade and Commerce-and I am sorry he is not here tonight-is able to use these estimates for the purpose of doing things for which there is no legislative authority whatever. Hon. members may remember that on April 7 of last year there was under discussion an item of some $800,000 in connection with the Canadian Commercial Corporation, I think; and after a great deal of wiggling the minister admitted in effect that there was no authority for it. But he said, "If parliament approves, the item will be confirmed by parliament." In other words, in effect he said, "We bring it' in here and if it is approved, all right; it doesn't matter whether or not we have authority for it."
I am just making the point that there is no real discussion; that everything goes; that estimates are brought in here as government measures; and that as far as I can see our procedure in dealing with these estimates comes close to being a solemn farce. They are a means of eliciting a certain amount of information; they provide an opportunity to make speeches which we hope will be read by the people at home, and all that sort of thing; but as far as service of the state is concerned, it just is not so. It is under those circumstances that I want to ask the minister what he proposes to do here. As was pointed out this afternoon, we have been refused a committee, and that is that. Now I want to know how we are going to have any real discussion unless we get the information; and how is the information to be given? Are we to get the facts here in this committee of the whole? I think we all know how difficult it is to get information here, with no experts present. We would require a system of orderlies running in and out if there were a real desire on the part of the government to answer questions. Of course what really happens is that we get tired, tempers get short, and eventually out of sheer fatigue the items go through. There is no really satisfactory discussion; there cannot be under such a procedure.
In the case of these defence estimates that is accentuated over and over again, because here we have many items on which, of all things, we need expert assistance. This afternoon, when my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo had finished speaking, the minister

very generously thanked him for his suggestions, and if I remember his words correctly even termed them constructive suggestions; yet neither the hon. member for Nanaimo nor anyone else in this house is to have an opportunity of talking with any of the experts. I will have a little more to say about that a little later on.
What has the minister said to us in answer to the complaints? He said one or two things. If I remember well, he said that never had so much information been given as now. I am not particularly interested in that statement. It is possible that we may have passed out of black darkness into twilight, and I am not going to argue on that; but I submit that what we want is light-I mean information in a way it has not been given before. I think that situation has to be faced.
Now let us look at these figures; let me look at this $80 million I mentioned previously. I am going to be in my riding tomorrow morning, and I have a great many intelligent electors there. I can imagine one of them saying, "What about this $80 million? Do you know anything about that?" I will have to say, "No, I don't know much about airplanes." Then I can imagine him asking, "Then how are you going to vote on that? Is anybody going to know anything about it"? I would reply, "The minister is going to tell us about it." Then my questioner might say, "Well, is the minister an expert?" I would have to reply, "Well, no; the minister very frankly said he was not an expert." Then I think my friend would say, "Well, have you any experts in the house at all, either on your own side or on the other side?" I would say, "Yes, we certainly have on our side some I would consider experts, such as the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Calgary East, and I think there are others I could name. I am quite sure in the other corners of the house there are some people of the same kind, who could be useful in that discussion." Then I can imagine my questioner going on and questioning me making me look very silly, and finally saying, "Do you mean to tell me you are going to pass an item of $80 million, not knowing a thing about it at first hand, except what somebody tells you, and that has been passed on by somebody else?" I think he would go on to say, "That is a funny kind of joint you are running down there," and he would be quite right.
I ask the minister what he would have to say to that, because as far as I can see that is the position we are in. My questioner, I think, might very well say, "Well, it would seem a sensible thing to get together a group of these men who are more expert than you
Supply-National Defence are and have them sit in with the minister's experts and discuss the whole thing." I would reply, "Yes, I should think that would be a very reasonable thing indeed, but the government would not allow that. That is the kind of government we have. They are so much better than the rest of us they do not need to discuss these matters with anyone in the house outside the government ranks."
And they even have study groups.

I wish I knew more about that study group. I really think the minister ought to help us a little on this. We are very modest people over here in the opposition. We read what the Prime Minister said the other day, that there are no people in Canada to be compared with the members of the cabinet; and I imagine he might include the parliamentary assistants as well. He did not say that, but they are a nice lot of chaps. And of course we know that he is going to Toronto, to that great university which I sometimes think is too pleased with itself, so that from time to time I have to remind it that smaller places have better quality than larger places; still it is a great university. The Prime Minister is to be there to establish the fact that there is no alternative to the present government. So, as I say, we approach this in a very modest manner; we are only asking for help in doing our duty, as far as it is possible for us to do it.
Just farm boys trying to get along.

That is right. Just here I should like to correct one misapprehension the minister is under. This will involve going back for just a moment to the debate on the proposal to establish a committee. Of course I am not going to debate that question at all; I am just putting this on the record because apparently the minister had it in his mind that what we suggested here was something that would require a constitutional change.

Mr. Chairman, I think we must have a stop to this sort of effort to restore the debate to the position it was in before the decision was arrived at by this house that there would be no committee. Therefore, I suggest to you that the hon. member is out of order.

May I rise to point out that the motion that was before the house, and on which the house voted, was a motion for a general committee to inquire into the Department of National Defence and the connected problems of defence. There is absolutely nothing in the decision that was reached then

Supply-National Defence which would prevent the hon. member reviewing that decision. Certainly, there could be nothing in that decision to prevent the suggestion now that there should be a committee to consider defence estimates; that was not the motion before the house.

Now, coming back, Mr. Chairman, to the suggestion that would lead to the defence estimates going to a committee-as I said, I am not arguing about the other committee at all. I am putting something on the record, because I think the minister would like to withdraw a mistaken statement, if he thinks it is mistaken after hearing what I read to him. It is very brief, but I want to read what was said by the leader of the opposition on November 18 last:
If the answer to the request is there can be no committee-

Really, Mr. Chairman, we have to have a ruling on this. Either this parliament decides one thing once, or it continues endlessly debating the same thing day after day, and week after week, after parliament has decided it. I do not think that makes sense. It is against the rules of the house, and I ask for a ruling.

speechtext: I think the hon. member is out of order, because he is referring to a previous debate; that is out of order.
It is from the last session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry, but the hon. member cannot review a debate which has already been decided. I cite Beauchesne, third edition, 245:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded; and it would be little use in preventing the same question from being offered twice in the same session if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again and again.
Mr. Chairman, I think-

Very well, Mr. Chairman, I appeal the ruling.

Mr. Speaker resumed the chair and the chairman of the committee made the following report:
Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) was discussing the advisability of appointing a special committee to consider national defence estimates. I ruled the discussion out of order as reviving a debate already concluded.
Mr. Speaker put the question as follows:
Mr. Dion from the committee of supply reports that in the committee of supply Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) was discussing the advisability of appointing a special committee to consider national defence estimates. The chairman ruled the discussion out of order as reviving a debate already concluded. From this ruling the leader of the opposition appealed to the house.
I was paired with the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner). Had I voted I would have voted aginst the ruling.
I was paired. Had I voted I would have voted against the chairman's ruling.

I declare the chairman's ruling confirmed.
And the house having resumed in committee:

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry for this interlude, when I thought I was getting on with the minister so well. I now begin again.
I wish to point out the situation as I see it. What we are now faced with is a situation where the only members who will be able to have a chance to form an opinion on these matters at first hand will be the minister, and anyone else with whom he chooses to take counsel

I presume his assistant, and possibly one or t"-o o+hers. The rest will have to form their opinions at second hand. Apparently they will have to judge what the experts say and think and feel entirely on what the minister tells them they say and think and feel.
I am not able to understand why this should be so. It does not make sense to me, at all. I would like to give an illustration from the business world. But first I would like to repeat a suggestion which has already come out, that although we may not have a committee on defence, which has been decided against, we could have the other different kind of committee to which the leader of the opposition referred, merely a committee to consider these accounts.
I wish now to give my illustration from the business world. I ask members to consider a situation where the general manager of a company-and I compare the minister to a general manager who, after all, holds a most dignified position-comes to his directors. I should think that in a sense the members of the House of Commons might be in the same position as the directors of the company. Then the general manager says that he proposes to embark the company upon very heavy expenditures in connection with very
Supply-National Defence difficult and important matters of a highly technical nature. He shows no sign whatever of allowing any of the directors to form any opinion, or to form their own opinions from a direct contact with the experts.
Finally I would suppose that some of the directors might suggest that it would be very desirable to have a committee of the board, and it might be suggested that there were on the board men who had expert knowledge- indeed, perhaps some with greater knowledge than the general manager-on these particular technical matters. It is suggested that a committee be formed so that these men may make up their own minds from firsthand evidence and be in a position to advise their colleagues on the board.
I suggest that that is exactly what has been put to the minister, and what I am putting again. We will suppose the general manager refuses. He says no, it is better that he should see only these experts. I would ask hon. members to consider what would ever prompt a general manager to make such an answer as that. Would it be, perhaps, that he was afraid?

Mr. Chairman, surely the hon. member has had enough experience in the House of Commons to know that he cannot do indirectly what he has failed to do directly. I suggest that the hon. member has been out of order in all his remarks since the last vote.

Mr. Chairman, I submit that all I am doing is to suggest to hon. members an analogy with what we are being asked to do. I am suggesting to the minister that he might advise some way whereby we in this House of Commons could discharge our duty.

I can answer that right now. By following the ordinary rules of parliament, the practice since this parliament has been in existence is to have the estimates discussed before the whole committee of parliament, as they have been tonight, and as they always have been.
But surely I am entitled to point out that that procedure has disadvantages. That is all I am doing.
Mr. Chairman, I ask that you rule the hon. member out of order, because he is suggesting some other procedure, which has already been voted on by this house within this week.

Is it out of order for anyone to discuss national defence at all? Apparently it must be.
