Mr. Chairman, the house, when it was meeting, decided that the estimates of the Department of National Defence would be called, beginning with item 202, and that is the item under discussion. And I suggest that every word said by the hon. member for Greenwood is out of order. We are discussing item 202, and following items.

I do not
know much about the rules of this house.
We realize that.

There is one thing that is perfectly clear and that is that on the first item of any department there has been wide opportunity for discussion. I submit that the minister is entirely wrong in saying one has to be tied to any narrow compass. All I am asking the minister to do is to see if he can think of some way to enable us to be provided with some information. As I say, he may have some entirely different method that I have not thought of at all.
I am only putting this forward. I am only making a suggestion which I do not think he will want to have denied. We on this side of the house feel that we are being treated in a most unfair manner. That is all I am saying, and I should like to go on.
I should like to give this illustration from business. I have given you the situation

of a general manager who comes to his directors and asks them to form an opinion without their having an opportunity to see the experts. I say that that is a most undesirable situation. I say further that I have no doubt we have experts in this house and I hope that in some way which the minister may devise better than I it will be possible for those men to form their opinions through direct contacts and then let the rest of us have the benefit of their advice. I cannot for the life of me believe that when the minister thinks this over he will not desire to do that if he can. If he does not, all 1 can say is that he is not the man I thought he was.
Oh, oh.

Let me take back those words and just say that I would have thought that the minister would be anxious to meet us to the extent of letting us arrive at an independent judgment on these important matters. That is all I am asking and I do not think it is unreasonable. There ought to be some way of doing it. I do not know whether it is good parliamentary procedure, but I do know it is common sense. I believe every voter in this country will say it is common sense.
I think I am stating the situation fairly, and the minister can correct me if I am not, when I say that the minister is proposing that no member of this house except perhaps himself and the parliamentary assistant, and maybe one or two members of the government, shall have any direct contact with the sources of information, that is to say, with the experts. If that is a fair statement, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, then 1 just cannot believe that it makes common sense, or that the minister will want to stick to that.
Why should he not want people to talk with the experts? Is it because he has the same fear as the general manager?

I ha-ve already raised this question and the hon. gentleman, for whom I have the greatest respect based on a friendship of 25 years, should know that he cannot get around the rules of this house in the way he is trying. He cannot raise this question again and again and again.
And again.
This is a new method of dealing with the rules of the house and the estimates that are referred to the committee of the whole house on supply.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is high time we understood exactly what the procedure is. You will recall that the last estimates that were brought before the house were those of the Department of External Affairs. In calling those estimates, just as in calling these, the long accepted practice was adopted of the minister making a statement. Following that statement, those who cared to follow in the debate did so. It was clearly understood, and understood from the moment the minister began to speak, that, when the debate on the statement made by the minister ended, the motion would then be dealt with to refer the items to a committee.
The procedure now before us is precisely the same. The minister has used, and properly used, the calling of these estimates before the committee as a means of making his statement on national defence. He has covered the whole ambit of national defence, far beyond this single item. The practice is clearly established that the debate then continues in relation to the speech of the minister, and when that debate is concluded the ''terns are proceeded with item by item.
Supply-National Defence
That was the procedure followed in the case of the Department of External Affairs. It' was so clearly followed that we now have an adjourned motion in relation to those estimates which will be resumed at a later date, not to deal with the item itself but with the debate which was continuing in relation to the statement by the minister. That is what we are doing now and it would be a violation of long accepted practice to suggest that we depart from that at this moment.

If I may speak on the point of order, I could not agree more with the leader of the opposition, because he has stated the position perfectly. I am completely in agreement with him except when we go on to discuss, as I submit the hon. member for Greenwood has been doing for some time, something which is in addition and which has been decided in this house by a vote this week. He is now getting to the point where he is wasting our time and where he is out of order.
Apparently the minister has entirely misunderstood me. He thinks I am still talking about a committee. What I am doing-
What are you doing?

Oh, Fraser Valley again. What I am doing is merely to ask the minister for help. I am merely asking the minister to exercise some common sense where we can be sensibly within the rules. I have very little more to say, but I do want to go back to what I think is a most interesting point. I am sure the members of the house should all be interested. Why is it that the minister feels that none of us must talk to the experts?
Let me say quickly that we recognize that there are certain matters of security. Of course we do. We are not irresponsible. We know there are certain things that cannot be disclosed and we also know that those are the minister's responsibility. But I am asking why it is that nobody can talk to the experts. Is it because the minister, like my imaginary general manager, is afraid that the experts may say things that are different from what they have said to him?

Mr. Chairman, I just ask the Minister of Public Works this question. Suppose the Minister of National Defence wanted to bring somebody in here. It has been done before in wartime. Let me repeat that I do not think the minister listened to me as carefully as I wish he had.
Never done.

I want to bring up the point that we are now left in the position where no one except the minister can see these experts. I want to raise that point, and that is my last point. I cannot see any reason why it should not be done, and I hope when the minister thinks it over he will not feel it is desirable to pull down the blinds and keep out the light.

Mr. Chairman, it is my privilege tonight to say a few words as to defence and the armed forces of Canada on these estimates. I think it is most appropriate that I, as the member for Kingston City, should have a few words to say as to this matter. I wish to say that I consider it a great honour to represent Kingston City not only because of its historical, educational and military background but also because it was once represented by the late Hon. Norman Rogers, who was formerly minister of national defence. I think it is fitting at this time that I should pay a tribute to this man because time does not lessen a tribute paid to so great a statesman.
It is also fitting that I should direct the attention of the house to the Royal Military College at Kingston. The Royal Military College is not exactly within the confines of my constituency, but just beyond the boundary thereof. I should also like to say that it is not the only military establishment in the city of Kingston and vicinity, a fact of which many hon. members are well aware. At this time I wish to direct the attention of the house particularly to the Royal Military College in order that hon. members may be aware of its activities and the good that it is doing in the building of Canada as a nation. I also wish to direct attention to a statement of the hon. member for Middlesex East to be found at page 90 of Hansard of the 21st of February of this year. He said that he considers the

education of officers at the Royal Military College at Kingston as a waste, and that we might better train officers in the C.O.T.C. at universities. It is not my intention to make any personal attack on the hon. member for Middlesex East because I am quite sure that he was sincere and earnest in his remarks. He was directing attention to expenditures which he considered exorbitant in the education of young officers at the Royal Military College. He expressed the view that they could be trained elsewhere.
To understand fully the activities of the Royal Military College I think it is necessary to make a slight review of its history and the activities which are carried on there for which our money is being spent. It was brought into being in 1876 and is the oldest military school in Canada. I may say that in past years a number of its graduates were among the first presidents of the engineering institute. It is also a point of history that the stone frigate which was built in 1820 is still used, and is one of the main buildings at the Royal Military College.
Geographically the college is situated on a projection of land which ends in Point Frederick. On the east is Navy bay and on the west the Cataraqui river. The college is also blessed with many fine limestone buildings which at the present time are being extended. There is a dormitory now under construction for the accommodation of cadets who are being trained at the college to be officers. We must consider the military and educational role that the Royal Military College has played in making a nation of Canada. I might mention to the house that a large number of ex-cadets of the college have died on active service. Many of them have risen high in our present defence organizations. Up to last year there were only 2,032 graduates of Royal Military College since its opening in 1876 arid 272 ex-cadets have died on active service. The proportion of its graduates killed on active service is greater than in any other Canadian university.
I think it is also significant to point out that between 85 and 90 per cent of the ex-cadets of military age were on active service during world war I and world war II. It has produced renowned and successful leaders, which is borne out by the fact that of the relatively small number of graduates it has produced three generals, nine lieutenant-generals and forty-six major-generals.
We should also consider the use to which the Royal Military College was put during the war. There was very little maintenance carried on during that time and we should consider what it is necessary to do now. It ceased to operate early in the war and was used for
Supply-National Defence officer training for special courses. I am sure many hon. members of the house attended them. It reopened in September, 1948, and it is significant to note that it reopened as a joint services college. The courses are designed to train officer cadets for the active and reserve forces of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force. I might say at this point, with reference to the expenditure on the training of officers in Canada, there is also the Royal Roads college which has a two-year course. The distinction is that the Royal Military College of Kingston has a four-year course. With the exception of the final year, this college has no summer term. Each year consists of eleven months of instruction, and the year is divided into three terms, fall, winter and summer.
During the fall and winter terms 85 per cent of the instruction is on academic subjects and the remainder on service topics, including physical training. The summer term is devoted entirely to practical service training at the various armed forces establishments, and with different units to which a cadet may be attached during the summer in order to get what we might call his practical training in the services. This summer term of practical training must be taken by all cadets who successfully complete the fall and winter terms, and commences in May, continuing until late in August. In this term the cadets follow courses of practical military training in their own service, whatever it may be. The pay for the cadet during the summer term amounts to $153 per month plus board, lodging and clothing.
Naval cadets are appointed to the naval reserve with the rank of cadet. Studies include instruction in navigation, seamanship, engineering, communication, gunnery and other subjects. The practical aspects of the naval instruction are emphasized in the four to six weeks they spend at sea during the summer on board ships of the Royal Canadian Navy.
Army cadets are enrolled in the C.O.T.C. and are given the status of second lieutenants during training. Officer cadets receive training in the branch of the army in which they will be commissioned. Training is conducted at the various schools under a progressive syllabus during the three years of summer training. On completion of the three years of the C.O.T.C. program an officer cadet is qualified as a lieutenant in the active force or as a captain in the reserve force if he so chooses, which I will speak about later.
Air force cadets are appointed to the R.C.A.F. supplementary reserve class "F", with the rank of cadet. They receive flying

Supply-National Defence training as pilots, navigation officers or radio officers during the three years of summer training before graduation from college; and on completion of their course are awarded their wings and join whatever branch of the air force they may prefer.
I wish now for a moment to deal with the details of these courses which these young men receive. The first two years are the same at both Royal Military College and Royal Roads. The third and fourth years of a general or engineering course are taken at R.M.C., with specialization starting in the third year. Four to five hours a week in all courses are devoted to physical training and service subjects. I think this is significant. We must realize that if these cadets who take their third and fourth years at R.M.C. are to be properly trained in engineering, there must be reasonable capital expenditures as far as laboratories are concerned.
It will have been noted that since the beginning of the year Canadian newspapers and magazines have been carrying advertisements with respect to enlistment at R.M.C. We as Canadians cannot but feel proud of the Royal Military College because of the democratic way in which the cadets are chosen. The requirements for admission are high, but the procedure is democratic. A candidate to become a cadet must be a Canadian citizen or other British subject normally resident in Canada. Candidates must have reached their sixteenth year but not their twentieth birthday on the first day of January preceding entry. Naval applicants, except in the case of candidates from French classical colleges, must not have reached their nineteenth birthday on January 1. A high standard of physical fitness is required of all candidates, and I am sure we will all agree this is very necessary for anyone about to enter His Majesty's service. The examinations are held at convenient centres by boards consisting of service medical officers. Candidates are also required to appear before a regional board of service officers and college officials for a personal interview. Both medical examinations and personal interviews take place each year about the first week of July. I think we might condense it by saying that any boy, no matter who he is, providing he is physically fit and has a sufficiently high academic standing, may be admitted as a cadet at R.M.C. Half the candidates are selected under a provincial quota determined by population, while the remainder are selected in open competition. In both cases selection is based upon the academic standing and the recommendation of the service board as to the physical and personal characteristics of candidates. Later I will discuss the matter of the fees which the candidates must pay the receiver general. I 
am quite sure that hon. members will agree that they are sufficiently low that almost any lad who can qualify as to physical fitness and academic standing may become a cadet at R.M.C.
Before any member of this house or any Canadian citizen attacks the expenditures being made by the Canadian people to maintain the Royal Military College, that person should carefully weigh the advantages of this college to Canada as a whole. They should also make a comparison with other forms of military education such as the C.O.T.C. which, it is granted, does an excellent job at the universities, where education in arts, letters and sciences is predominant. At R.M.C. cadets receive an education in arts, letters and sciences and a military education, with none of these being stressed at the expense of the others.
I should like to review briefly the role of R.M.C. It is a military educational establishment maintained primarily for the training of cadets for entry into the commissioned ranks of His Majesty's service. It has the educational status of a university college, and is a full member of the national conference of Canadian universities. It is one of the three sources for the production of officers for our armed forces in Canada; and in considering the Royal Military College I think it important to remember that it does not depend upon quantity but rather upon the quality of its products. I believe we should pay attention to the fact that it sets a standard pattern which serves as a yardstick for the various officer production schemes we have in Canada.
The unification of the services is one of the latest developments in military science. In this development R.M.C., in its training of .cadets for all armed services, plays a key part. It is appropriate this week that I should speak about R.M.C. and its importance in the national life of Canada, because a week ago tonight the West Point hockey team motored to Kingston to play the annual hockey game with the cadets of R.M.C. It is regretted, but shows signs of good sportsmanship, that those boys came up here with the idea of winning their fourth straight hockey game over R.M.C. I must say they did very well this time, as the minister stated the other day, but West Point were repelled by R.M.C. by a score of 6 to 4.
By way of deviation, may I stress the importance of the hockey game between West Point and R.M.C. These boys came from the United States to play against R.M.C. They spent the week end with our cadets, dined with them, were shown around the buildings, went on parade with them, and went to church with them. We in Canada

should feel grateful we have a college of that nature, because here we find friendships being established between the future generals, admirals, and air marshals of these two great American countries. Regardless of who won the game, I am sure that both countries will be better off in the future, owing to this intermingling of our defence leaders of tomorrow.
If we are to fully appreciate the value of R.M.C., one must look at least 50 years into the future of Canada. No one knows what lies in store for Canada, and what troubles are ahead. We do know that between world wars I and II there appeared in our universities an almost complete lack of military training, and such periods will likely return. Therefore, we should be congratulated on having two military colleges.
The Royal Military College has a large investment in buildings, starting with a stone frigate in 1820. It also has an extremely capable staff of civil servants, backed by a powerful alumni who, after leaving college, take an active part in defence developments in Canada. They are also interested in the service training in Canada, and I believe are always available for their suggestions. There is another role which R.M.C. plays in the national life of Canada. It helps to weld together the English and French-speaking Canadians. French is a compulsory subject at R.M.C., and the college attracts a good percentage of French-speaking cadets. I believe statistics show that last year around 15 per cent of the cadets were Frenchspeaking, and it is expected that this proportion will increase with time.
Prior to this last war we often heard that if there were a world war II it would be a war of great scientific proportions. Towards the end of world war II we learned of the atom bomb. Now we are speaking of the H-bomb. If there is a world war III it will call for a greater number of scientifically trained officers than world war II. Every dollar spent on capital equipment for R.M.C. in peacetime increases our war potential. It could be compared to the British Military College of Science, a unit with a highly qualified technical staff whose teaching and research facilities, on very short notice, could undertake the training of a large number of technical officers for the services. R.M.C. is like the military college of science, in that it trains officers for the technical corps and the army, but R.M.C. differs in that it does the same for the navy and the air force. In so far as research is concerned, R.M.C. and the military college of science are parallel.
There is no more important investment that Canada could make in peacetime than the education of an officer, no matter what
Supply-National Defence service he chooses to enter. Such an officer corps undoubtedly becomes the nucleus of our forces in wartime. When we compare the cost we might say, by way of comparison, that one jet fighter and its accessories would buy the equipment for all the laboratories at R.M.C., and maintain them for a period of 10 years. At this particular time in our history, the value to the services of the engineering graduates trained on this equipment, over a period of 20 years, would certainly be greater than the value obtained from one jet fighter, which might either be destroyed or become obsolete in a few years.
It is important, both in Canada and in the United States, that there be a means of introducing into our universities compulsory physical discipline and training, in order that we can make our young men physically, mentally and spiritually fit. R.M.C. is one of the few educational establishments on a military and university level which fulfils this role. The quality of officers produced at the service college will depend, in the long run, on the quality of the staff and cadets that can be attracted to the college. Unless both the staff and cadets are of high calibre, there is no way of producing a product of the high calibre required to form the nucleus of our wartime army or to lead our peacetime army. Upon admission to R.M.C. or Royal Roads, each officer cadet must undertake, upon graduation, to serve as a commissioned officer in one of the three services, either in the active or in the reserve force.
A brilliant young cadet, keen to make a reputation in civilian life, plays an important role in the well-being of R.M.C. He acts as a leader and pace-setter while at R.M.C., and builds up the prestige of the college in civilian life. Experience shows that this type of graduate finds time to serve with distinction in the reserve force in whatever part of Canada he may choose to reside. Again, this contributes to the standardization of our training.
I have mentioned previously that Kingston is an educational city. I am sure you are all aware that Queen's university is located there, and I know that many graduates of Queen's are on the floor of this house. But Queen's plays a greater part than merely being an educational institution. It is a most important factor in making R.M.C. an attractive seat of learning. It is significant to note that the faculty at R.M.C. takes an active part in all the activities at Queen's. Last year five of the R.M.C. staff lectured at Queen's, and several members of the Queen's staff lectured at R.M.C. It must be realized, though, that such an association will last only as long as R.M.C. contributes its share of instructors equal in professional status to the instructors

Supply-National Defence at Queen's. I think it is most important, therefore, that the staff at R.M.C. be as well qualified as the staff at Queen's, or equivalent universities, in order that we may maintain a high standard of training for our officer cadets. If the staff at R.M.C. is to be as good as at other universities, it is only natural that those in charge at R.M.C. must be prepared to pay an equivalent salary. I understand the staff members of this military college are not allowed to take consulting work in the summer, but are retained in research or training in summer courses.
Canada has traditionally based her defence on a nucleus force built up in peacetime. We are also dependent upon voluntary enlistment. I think it is to the advantage of the defence of Canada that our nucleus force, either active or reserve, has available as officers those trained in a standard pattern, which makes the unification of the services easier. The member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) has stated in substance that it would be better to train officers in the C.O.T.C., at a cost of $500 per cadet, than by operating R.M.C. at a cost of $30,000 per officer. I think, before we can accept his view, we should review the cost to the government of training a cadet at R.M.C. According to the information which I have obtained, there are at present 170 cadets attending that college. You will recall that it only reopened in the fall of 1948, and it was estimated that for the next four years there would be 100 entrants in each class. The plan therefore would be to accommodate 400 cadets who, it is estimated, will be in attendance in the year 1951. The full cost of operating R.M.C. at full strength would be in the neighbourhood of $1 million per year, exclusive of capital costs. If the fees which are paid to the receiver general, and of which I will speak later, are deducted plus a reasonable deduction for the use of equipment, staff and other facilities of R.M.C. by the services, defence research boards and other government departments during the three and a half months in the summer when the college is free of cadets, we therefore could estimate the cost of training the 400 cadets at $740,000. The cost per cadet per annum therefore would be in the neighbourhood of $1,850.
In the brief submitted to the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, dated July, 1949, it is pointed out that the cost of training a medical student in Canada is approximately $1,200 per year. When the cost of medical research and maintenance of medical research is considered, which is important, the cost of training this medical student would be $1,600 per year. Of this total annual cost, I think we will find from that report that the student

pays 25 per cent. Therefore I think that this sum of $1,600 for training of a medical student should be borne in mind in the consideration of the training of a cadet at R.M.C. As 1 have said, the training of the cadet can be estimated at $1,850 per year per cadet; but at R.M.C. it is necessary for the cadets to live in dormitories in order that they have the advantages of a military mess. In other words, it is a military unit in order to train them as young officers. This part of their training normally should cost in the neighbourhood of $550 per year. When this is deducted from the $1,850, we get a figure of $1,300 per year per cadet. We should also consider during that period of time-those eight and a half months when they are taking training there-the staff is also carrying on research to the benefit of the defence research board.
Let us now consider the fees which are paid by cadets attending R.M.C. There is an annual tuition fee of $100 payable in advance, and in addition a charge to cover the partial cost of room, uniforms, laundry, books, etc., of $450 per cadet in the first year and $200 in the subsequent years. There is another $30 which is the normal athletic fee paid at other universities. Therefore, to sum it up, each cadet pays to the receiver general in his first year $580 and in his subsequent years the sum of $330. It is also to be noted that he receives transportation costs of $25 once a year from his home to the college.
I am sure that the hon. member for Middlesex East cannot say that the expenditures entailed in educating a cadet at R.M.C. are exorbitant. I agree with him that there have been large capital expenditures this year owing to the preparation of laboratories for 300 to 400 students in the year 1951; but I think it is proper to assume that these capital expenditures will not go up, and such expenditures made in peacetime are war potentials for the future. We must also bear in mind that during wartime R.M.C. was used for officer training and its laboratories and equipment were put to use by the officers trained there; and I doubt very much if there was much time for maintenance in those days. If we did not have R.M.C. or if we did not have a college for training our officers, as has been suggested, I think that we would be unique among the leading countries of the world, because most countries have their officer training schools. The United States has West Point, England has Sandhurst and the Military College of Science and Belgium has its Military Academy. I think it is also significant to compare the establishment of the total staff of R.M.C., including cleaners and cooks, up to strength, and students; I think we shall find that the ratio is [DOT] 7 of staff to 1 of

the cadets, which is about one-half of the figure for West Point and much less than that for Sandhurst. The pre-war figures at R.M.C. were -85 to 1. We shall therefore be running a post-war R.M.C. with a smaller comparative staff per cadet; and from what I can find out, R.M.C. is being operated at the present time at the lowest staff-student ratio of any military college.
It may also be of interest for the committee to know that during last summer, which was the first summer of vacation since R.M.C. reopened in 1948, an all arms course was carried on by the army at R.M.C. This, I understand, was mostly for students who had three years C.O.T.C., and who spent their fourth summer, for final training, in the college grounds. I might say that we must always beai in mind that this is one way to train our officers in which we can have one standard and have unification of the services.
I also wish to make a short remark with respect to a report in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 4, 1950, of a speech made by the hon. member for Middlesex East in which he states that, as he saw it, the R.M.C. is merely creating and nurturing a military caste in Canada, that it might better be closed and the training of army officers turned over to the universities. As one who resides in
Supply-National Defence Kingston, I wish to say that I have many friends and neighbours there who are graduates of R.M.C. and are connected with it. There are many other such persons in the city. I doubt whether there is a larger group or aggregation of cadets and staff of a military institution in any other place in Canada; and I have not found these gentlemen to be as described, a caste separate and distinct from other people or other citizens. They seem to be successful, to take an interest in civil life and to retain a keen interest in army affairs. I might say that they are a benefit to any community, whether in the active army or civilians in the reserve force, or retired. They are also among the best of citizens and are a great contribution to the backbone of any community.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
